title: Chat — Service Health
description:
Triage surface for the chat platform: an alert fires, you open this, and you read down until you know which layer is broken. Row 1 is what users experience, row 2 is whether the processes are healthy, and the collapsed rows are the drill-down.

Core path (the Core path unhealthy tile): message-gatekeeper, broadcast-worker, message-worker, roomlist-worker, notification-worker.

Server-side NATS, MongoDB and Cassandra health belongs to the teams that run them; everything here is the client side.

list.name: datasource
list.label: Site
list.description: Each site runs its own Prometheus, so selecting the datasource selects the site. There is deliberately no site variable.

list.name: service
list.label: Service
list.description: Filters the application metrics only. The resource table and the ranked CPU/memory panels come from cAdvisor, which labels by container rather than service_name, and always show every container so a service cannot be hidden by a filter that does not know its name.

panels.title: Core path unhealthy
panels.description: Replicas that should be running and are not, restricted to the five services on the send path: message-gatekeeper, broadcast-worker, message-worker, roomlist-worker, notification-worker. A message that misses any of them is not accepted, delivered, persisted or notified. Non-zero here means act now.

panels.title: All deployments unhealthy
panels.description: Unavailable replicas across every deployment in the namespace, with no allowlist, so a newly added service is counted here even before anyone classifies it. Read it together with the tile on the left: the same number means the problem is on the send path.

panels.title: API error rate
panels.description:
Failed calls as a percentage of all calls, HTTP and NATS request/reply together. HTTP counts 5xx only -- a 4xx is the client being told no, not the service failing. NATS counts any call that carried an error.type, which the semantic convention omits on success.

A family with no series contributes nothing rather than voiding the whole tile, so a site that serves only NATS traffic still gets a number. When neither family is present the tile reads NO DATA, not 0% -- nothing scraped is not the same as nothing failing.

targets.expr: 100 * ((sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"$namespace", service_name=~"$service",http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0)) + (sum(rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"$namespace", service_name=~"$service",error_type!=""}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0))) / ((sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"$namespace", service_name=~"$service"}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0)) + (sum(rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"$namespace", service_name=~"$service"}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0)))

panels.title: Circuit breakers open
panels.description:
Breakers currently open or half-open across the six services that use pkg/circuitbreaker. This is the fastest answer to "which dependency is fenced" -- no datastore exporter can see it, because a breaker is application state.

A breaker publishes its state only on the first transition, so a service whose breakers have never tripped has no series at all. NO DATA here means nothing has ever tripped, which is the healthy case.

panels.title: Request rate
panels.description: Traffic, the golden signal that is missing from every error-only dashboard. A sudden drop is an outage upstream of these services -- and while it lasts the error rate falls too, because no requests are arriving to fail.

panels.title: HTTP errors by status class
panels.description: Status codes folded to their class. 5xx is the service failing; 4xx is the service correctly refusing, and during an auth incident 4xx rising is the symptom rather than the fault. Stacked so a rise in total volume is distinguishable from a change in mix.

panels.title: NATS RPC errors by type
panels.description: error.type is absent on a successful call, so every series here is a failure. unavailable and internal are the service breaking; not_found, forbidden, conflict and bad_request are it working correctly and saying no.

panels.title: HTTP latency
panels.description: p95 and p99 across all routes. Percentiles are interpolated inside a bucket and aggregated across pods, so read them for shape and movement. The top boundary is 10s: a p99 pinned there means "at least 10s", not 10s.

panels.title: NATS RPC latency
panels.description: p95 and p99 across all request/reply methods. Shares o11y's bucket boundaries with the HTTP histogram on purpose, so the two percentiles are directly comparable.

panels.title: Service resources
panels.description:
One row per container, from cAdvisor and kube-state. Sorted by restarts because that is the only column where any non-zero value is always a finding -- 80% CPU can be normal, three restarts never is. The graded columns have their own ranked views below.

Rows are containers, not services: the pod-level rollup (container="") and the pause container are excluded, so a pod with sidecars contributes one row per sidecar.

Restarts are counted inside the selected time range. A pod that was replaced takes its counter with it, so a service that crashed and was then rescheduled is undercounted here; the deploy markers and the availability tiles at the top cover that case.

targets.expr: 100 * sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD",resource="cpu"})

100 * sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval]))

100 * sum by (container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}) / sum by (container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD",resource="memory"})

panels.title: CPU: top 10 by % of limit
panels.description: Cores used against the container's CPU limit. High is not by itself a problem -- a service allowed two cores and using them is working. Read it next to the throttle panel: high CPU without throttling is healthy use of the budget.

targets.expr: topk(10, 100 * sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD",resource="cpu"}))

panels.title: CPU throttling: top 10
panels.description: Share of CFS periods in which the container was stopped after spending its quota. This is the panel CPU usage cannot replace: a bursty service can average 30% and still be frozen for most of every 100ms period, so latency moves while the CPU chart looks calm.

targets.expr: topk(10, 100 * sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Memory: top 10 by % of limit
panels.description: Working set against the container's memory limit. Working set is the number the kubelet uses for OOM kills and eviction, which is why it is here rather than usage (inflated by reclaimable page cache) or RSS (excludes it entirely).

targets.expr: topk(10, 100 * sum by (container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}) / sum by (container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace=~"$namespace", container!="", container!="POD",resource="memory"}))

panels.title: Go runtime configuration
panels.description:
Keyed by service_name from the OTel resource, so these rows come from a different label space than the resource table above and the two cannot be joined automatically -- the bot- and teams- deployments run the same binary under a different service_name than their container name. Compare against that table by eye.

Two rows are worth reading every time. GOMAXPROCS well above the container's CPU limit makes the Go scheduler open that many Ps against a fraction of a core, which is the most common cause of the throttling above. An empty GOMEMLIMIT means the runtime never feels the container's memory ceiling and will keep growing until the kernel intervenes -- the metric is only published when the limit is actually set, so blank is the finding.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: The signal is the slope, not the value. A count that climbs across deploy markers and never returns is a leak in a handler or consumer; a count that tracks traffic is normal. The table above gives the current number, this gives the direction.

panels.title: HTTP routes
panels.description: One row per registered route. Routes are templated by the gin middleware, so path parameters never become separate rows.

panels.title: NATS RPC methods
panels.description:
One row per service and rpc.method. The vocabulary is a curated enum mapped from the subject, and it only covers room-service, history-service and the teams routes: every call to user-service, search-service and media-service records rpc_method="unknown". Those rows are that service's whole request surface collapsed into one, which is why the table groups by service as well -- without it three services would share a single unknown row.

The router already computes a per-route wildcard pattern at registration; exporting it as a second label would give this table one row per API. That is a change in pkg/natsmetrics, not here.

targets.expr: 100 * sum by (service_name, rpc_method) (rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"$namespace", service_name=~"$service",error_type!=""}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (service_name, rpc_method) (rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"$namespace", service_name=~"$service"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Datastore operations
panels.description: Client-side operation rate by datastore. This is what our processes asked for, not what the servers did -- the MongoDB, Cassandra and Valkey teams own the server view. Operation names carry no database or collection label; traces are the only way down to that level.

panels.title: Datastore error ratio
panels.description: Share of client operations that returned an error. error_type exists only on failures, so the numerator selects it and the denominator does not.

panels.title: Datastore p99 latency
panels.description: Client-observed p99 per datastore, which includes the network and any driver retry. A gap between this and the server team's own latency panel is the round trip plus the retry, and that gap is the part we own.

panels.title: Connection pool queue depth
panels.description: Requests waiting for a pooled connection. The datastore can be perfectly healthy while this climbs -- it measures our side running out of connections, which no server-side dashboard can see. It is a count, so it is plotted apart from the timeout rate beside it.

panels.title: Connection pool checkout timeouts
panels.description: Checkouts that gave up waiting. Any sustained rate means requests are failing for lack of a connection rather than anything the datastore did, and it is the signal that pool sizing, not the database, is the constraint.

panels.title: JetStream consumer loops
panels.description: Whether each service's consumer loop can still receive. It does not restart itself: the loop returns on a terminal error and stays gone until the process does, so a lane that drops to DOWN stays there. This is the alive-but-not-consuming failure, and it is invisible to a liveness probe.

panels.title: NATS client connections
panels.description: Whether each service still holds a broker connection. The underlying metric counts live connections rather than reporting a boolean, so it is clamped to 1 here: the question this answers is connected or not, and the count itself is not meaningful on a dashboard.

panels.title: Circuit breakers
panels.description: Per service and breaker name. A breaker publishes only on transition, so a breaker that has never tripped has no lane here at all -- an empty panel is the healthy state, not missing instrumentation.
